diagnoses.description: `Graph.validate()` is advertised as validating graph integrity, but it only checks edge endpoint existence and does not validate key constraints that the task/evaluators commonly enforce (e.g., all nodes reachable from the first node). Using this validation as-is can allow structurally invalid graphs to pass "validate" while failing downstream constraints.

The implementation treats the special target `"End"` inconsistently across validation/serialization/visualization: `validate()` explicitly allows edges to point to `End` even when `End` is not present in `self.nodes`, `to_dict()`/`to_json()` will omit an `End` node unless the user added one, but `visualize()` always injects an `End` node into the DOT output. This can produce a JSON graph with dangling `to: "End"` references (depending on consumer expectations) and a DOT graph that does not faithfully represent the serialized JSON graph.

Dynamics description uses incorrect rotational kinematics by setting Euler angle derivatives equal to body angular rates (`Euler angle derivative = current angular velocity`). For ZYX Euler angles, `[φ̇, θ̇, ψ̇]` is not equal to `[p, q, r]` except under small-angle/approximate assumptions; using this as “nonlinear equations of motion” will yield wrong attitude evolution.

diagnoses.description: Rotational dynamics are described as `Angular velocity derivative = I⁻¹ M` while calling the model “nonlinear equations of motion”. This omits the standard rigid-body coupling term `ω × (I ω)` (i.e., `I ω̇ = M − ω×(Iω)`), which is a concrete modeling error for a supposedly nonlinear quadrotor simulator.

diagnoses.description: `sampling-and-indexing` treats interval end semantics as a free choice (inclusive vs. exclusive) and uses `sample_ids` as original video frame indices. In this task, instruction keys are defined on *sample indices* and intervals are explicitly *half-open* (end-exclusive), so this guidance can produce systematically mis-keyed or wrong-semantics JSON intervals.

`output-validation` validates instruction interval bounds against the video frame count `n` and enforces `end < n`, which is incompatible with this task’s definition (keys are *sample indices* and half-open intervals often use `end == num_samples`). It also allows `start==end` (empty intervals) and fails to assert that each JSON value is a `list` (iterating a string would incorrectly pass per-character checks).

`egomotion-estimation` decision sketch assigns labels only for `i>0`, which can omit coverage for sampled frame index 0 and/or conflate per-transition labels with per-frame interval labels. This conflicts with the task’s interval semantics example where `"0->1"` must label sampled frame 0, and with the skill’s own requirement that compressed intervals cover all sampled frames.

Incorrect LMP sign: the skill states LMPs are the duals of nodal balance constraints directly, but with the demonstrated balance constraint written as `pg_at_bus - pd == B @ theta` (i.e., load enters with a negative sign), the marginal cost of increasing load is the negative of the dual (LMP = -dual * baseMVA). Using `dual * baseMVA` will flip LMP signs.

Counterfactual congestion flag logic conflicts with the task contract: the skill computes `congestion_relieved = was_binding_in_base and not is_binding_in_cf`, but the task defines the flag based on whether the adjusted line is binding in the counterfactual ("true indicates not binding"), without requiring it to have been binding in the base case.

DC network modeling is incomplete for MATPOWER branch records: the B-matrix construction and line flow formulas ignore transformer tap ratios/phase shifts and also do not filter out out-of-service branches (BR_STATUS). This yields incorrect flows/constraints for transformers and can incorrectly include disconnected elements in the network model.

Economic dispatch snippet contains a concrete variable-name error: it defines `gens` but then uses `gen[8]`/`gen[9]` (undefined) when showing how to read PMAX/PMIN, which would cause runtime errors or mis-implementation if followed literally.

The provided “above-minimum” startup-capability linearization can fail to enforce a stated startup_limit when startup_limit < Pmin. The constraint is written on (p_above_min + reserve) and does not include the Pmin*u term, so it can allow actual output = Pmin during a startup period even if that exceeds startup_limit (i.e., it does not correctly encode a limit on total MW during startup in the above-minimum variable convention).

diagnoses.description: `save-plan` claims it "Uses `unified_planning.io.PDDLWriter`" to write a plan in "standard PDDL plan format". `PDDLWriter` is for emitting PDDL domain/problem text, not serializing a computed plan into a plain action-per-line plan file. This is likely to produce the wrong output format or fail at runtime, and it does not align with the task requirement of writing a textual plan (one action per line) to `plan_output`.

The plan-generation notes hard-code the default planner as `pyperplan`, but `pyperplan` is commonly limited to STRIPS-style fragments and may not support typical IPC Airport encodings that use richer PDDL requirements (e.g., ADL features, conditional effects, negative/disjunctive preconditions). This makes the documented default approach unreliable for the stated benchmark suite.

The “enum type” guidance is incorrect and the example does not compile: it recommends UPPERCASE case-object names and explicitly discourages PascalCase (which is the conventional Scala style for types/constructors). Additionally, the example defines `object BaseType` but never defines a `sealed trait BaseType`, so `case object STRING extends BaseType` refers to a non-existent type and will not compile.

Several Scala code examples reuse the same `val` name multiple times in the same snippet (e.g., defining `val doubled` twice, `val total` twice). As written, these snippets are non-compiling Scala and can mislead implementation or copy/paste usage.

The functional programming guide includes Scala 3-only syntax (`trait Show[A]:`, `given`, `using`) inside the skill bundle, which targets Scala 2.13 translation. Even though a Scala 2 alternative is shown later, including Scala 3 syntax in a primary translation skill risks producing non-compiling Scala 2.13 output.

The type-mapping table suggests mapping Python `None` directly to Scala `None` “(of type Option)”, which is misleading: `None` is only valid where the Scala type is `Option[T]`. For non-Option types, the appropriate guidance is to model absence as `Option[T]` rather than implying `None` is a general-purpose null substitute.
